pos: n. (religion misdirected; reverence given to what has no claim to it; rendering Greek deisidaimonia)
etymology: Latin superstitio, literally a standing over — the awe of the man who stands transfixed before what he fears. The Greek of Acts 25:19 is deisidaimonia, fear of the divinities, a word that can mean religiousness or dread according to the speaker.
biblical_def: Superstition is reverence bestowed where God has not placed it. Festus described the dispute between Paul and the Jews as “certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive” (Act 25:19) — a pagan magistrate's dismissal of a religion he could not follow. Paul at Athens used the kindred word of the city itself: “Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious” (Act 17:22), and then preached the unknown God they had an altar to. The Lord's diagnosis of religion gone wrong is the standing one: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superstition as excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples; belief in the direct agency of superior powers in extraordinary events; false religion; excessive nicety.
webster_full: SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples in the observance of religious rites not commanded, or of points of minor importance.
2. A reverence of beings not proper objects of reverence; false religion; false worship.
3. Rite or practice proceeding from excess of scruples in religion.
4. Excessive nicety; scrupulous exactness.
scriptures: But had certain questions against him of their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Gal 4:10
Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years.
corruption_summary: Superstition is imagined as the vice of the ignorant, and Scripture finds it in the temple, in Athens, and in the churches of Galatia.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is now used almost entirely of the uneducated — charms, ladders, black cats — and Scripture never uses it that way. Superstition in the Bible is a disorder of religion itself, and it appears among the most careful worshippers on record. The Pharisees washed, tithed the herbs of the garden, and counted paces on the sabbath, and the Lord's verdict on the whole apparatus was that they worshipped in vain, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. Superstition is not too little religion. It is religion aimed at something God did not command, performed with a scruple He never asked for.

Galatians 4:10 is the form it takes in a Christian congregation: ye observe days, and months, and times, and years — and Paul's response is not amusement but alarm, “I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain.” The observance was religious, sincere, and biblical in its raw materials, since the days and months came out of Moses; and it was a return to the weak and beggarly elements, because it was being kept as a ground of standing. That is the exact mechanism. A practice becomes superstitious not when it is old or ceremonious but when a man's peace begins to rest on it.

Athens shows the other end of the range, and Paul's tone there is worth learning. He calls the city too superstitious, and then walks its streets, reads its altars, quotes its poets, and preaches the resurrection from the one inscription that admitted ignorance. He does not despise the impulse; he redirects it. Superstition is the religious instinct running without revelation, and the answer to it is not less reverence but a right object, which is why the sermon ends at a Man whom God hath raised from the dead.
roots_summary: Greek deisidaimonia (G1175), fear of the divine, religiousness or superstition; deisidaimonesteros (G1174), too superstitious; ethelothreskeia (G1479), will-worship; mataios (G3152), vain.
roots_lines: Greek deisidaimonia (G1175) — superstition, religion; Acts 25:19 only.
Greek deisidaimonesteros (G1174) — too superstitious, very religious; Acts 17:22 only.
Greek maten sebontai (G3155, G4576) — in vain they worship; Matthew 15:9, Mark 7:7.
usage: “Questions against him of their own superstition” — a Roman governor's word for the gospel.
“Ye men of Athens… too superstitious” — the instinct redirected, not despised.
“Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” — the form it takes in a church.

pos: n. pl. (the appointed outward forms of worship; rendering Hebrew chuqqah, statute, and mishpat, ordinance)
etymology: Latin caerimonia, a sacred rite. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the passover: kept “according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof” (Num 9:3).
biblical_def: Ceremonies are the outward forms God appointed for the worship of the old covenant. Israel was to keep the passover “according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof” (Num 9:3), and the first covenant “had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary” (Heb 9:1) which “stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation” (Heb 9:10). Paul gives their status now: “let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ceremony as outward rite; external form in religion; the forms and rites prescribed by law or custom; outward forms of civility.
webster_full: CEREMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion.
2. Forms of civility; rules established by custom for regulating social intercourse.
3. Outward forms of state; the forms prescribed or established by order or custom.
scriptures: Num 9:3
In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it.
Heb 9:1
Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary.
Heb 9:10
Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.
Col 2:16
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
corruption_summary: The ceremonies are either revived as though Christ had not come or despised as though God had never given them.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed have divided the law of Moses into moral, judicial and ceremonial, and the ceremonial law is the part the Confession says is now abrogated — not because it was bad but because it was a shadow, and the body is of Christ. Colossians 2:17 does not disparage the sacrifices, the feasts, or the priesthood; it dates them. A shadow is cast by something real and is exactly the shape of it, which is why the epistle to the Hebrews reads Leviticus with such attention. What has ceased is not their truth but their use, and to reinstate them — an altar, a priesthood, a sacrifice, a holy day binding the conscience — is to prefer the outline to the figure that cast it.

The opposite error empties Christian worship of form altogether, on the theory that ceremony as such belongs to the old covenant. It does not. The Lord left two ordinances with visible matter in them, water and bread and wine, and commanded that they be kept; He appointed a day, a table, a washing, and a book to be read and preached. The Reformed principle is not that worship should have no form but that its forms should be those God has appointed — which is why the Confession is at once so severe about invented ceremonies and so exact about the two that remain.

Hebrews 9:10 puts the limit of the whole system in one phrase: imposed on them until the time of reformation. The ceremonies could reach meats, drinks, and washings; they could not reach the conscience, which is what the next verses say the blood of Christ does. Every ceremonial religion since, Roman or Protestant, has failed at the same boundary, and the test of any observance is whether it is doing what only blood can do.
roots_summary: Hebrew chuqqah (H2708), a statute, appointed thing; mishpat (H4941), ordinance, prescribed manner; Greek dikaioma (G1345), an ordinance; skia (G4639), a shadow.
roots_lines: Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — statute, ceremony; Numbers 9:3, 9:12, 9:14, Exodus 12:14.
Greek dikaioma (G1345) — ordinance, carnal ordinance; Hebrews 9:1, 9:10, Luke 1:6.
Greek skia (G4639) — shadow; Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5, 10:1.
usage: “According to all the ceremonies thereof” — the passover kept exactly.
“Imposed on them until the time of reformation” — the system with a date on it.
“A shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” — the outline and the figure.

pos: n. pl. (prescribed acts of worship; rendering Hebrew mishpat, the appointed manner)
etymology: Latin ritus, a religious usage. The Authorized Version has the word once, beside ceremonies, in the law of the passover.
biblical_def: A rite is an appointed act of worship, done in a prescribed manner. “In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it” (Num 9:3). The insistence on manner runs through the Law: Nadab and Abihu offered “strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not” and died (Lev 10:1–2); Uzzah steadied the ark and was struck, because the ark was to be borne on the shoulders of Levites (2Sa 6:6–7). Under the new covenant the Lord left two: baptism (Mat 28:19) and the Supper — “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rite as the manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept, or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty.
webster_full: RITE, n. The manner of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty. Rites are ceremonies of religion.
scriptures: Num 9:3
In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it.
Lev 10:1
And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not.
Lev 10:2
And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: The manner of worship is treated as a matter of taste, and the two men who improvised at the altar were carried out in their coats.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 10 is the shortest argument for the regulative principle in Scripture. Nadab and Abihu were priests, at the altar, offering incense to the true God, on the day of their consecration; the fire they used was one He commanded them not, and it killed them. The offence is defined by absence, not by prohibition — there was no verse forbidding that fire, and there did not need to be. Aaron held his peace. The Reformed conclusion is that in worship what God has not appointed He has not authorised, and the burden of proof lies on the innovation rather than on the objector.

Modern worship is largely governed by the opposite rule: whatever is not forbidden is permitted, and the question asked of a new practice is whether it works. That is the normative principle, and it is held sincerely by good men; but it is not the principle of Leviticus 10, and its results are visible. A congregation that has no test but effect will in time worship in whatever manner the age finds effective, and the manner will teach a doctrine that the pulpit has not examined.

The counter-corruption is a Reformed vice: to hold the regulative principle so tightly that the two ordinances Christ actually left are administered thinly and infrequently, while the energy goes into policing what others do. Numbers 9:3 is a command to keep the passover, and to keep it exactly; the exactness serves the keeping. A church that guards the manner and neglects the ordinance has the argument and not the meal.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpat (H4941), the appointed manner, ordinance; chuqqah (H2708), statute; Greek esh zarah is the Hebrew for strange fire, zar (H2114), foreign, unauthorised.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — ordinance, prescribed manner, rite; Numbers 9:3, 9:14, Exodus 26:30.
Hebrew zar (H2114) — strange, unauthorised; Leviticus 10:1, Numbers 3:4, 26:61.
Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.
usage: “According to all the rites of it” — the manner commanded with the meal.
“Which he commanded them not” — the offence defined by absence.
“This do in remembrance of me” — one of the two the Lord left.

pos: n. (want of reverence toward God; ungodliness in its active form)
etymology: Latin impietas, from in, not, and pietas, dutiful reverence — the failure of the debt a creature owes his Maker and a son his father.
biblical_def: Impiety is the absence of the reverence owed to God, and Scripture treats it as an act rather than a mood. Paul locates it at the head of the human case: “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness” (Rom 1:18) — ungodliness first, because the offence against God precedes the offence against men. Its mark is a refusal to glorify or thank: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” (Rom 1:21). The godly man's opposite instinct is named in Hebrews: let us serve God “with reverence and godly fear” (Heb 12:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impiety as ungodliness; irreverence towards the Supreme Being; contempt of the divine character and authority; an act of wickedness.
webster_full: IMPIETY, n. Ungodliness; irreverence towards the Supreme Being; contempt of the divine character and authority; neglect of the divine precepts.
2. An act of wickedness; an act of contempt for the laws or character of God.
scriptures: Rom 1:18
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness;
Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
Jud 1:15

To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.
Psa 36:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David the servant of the LORD. The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes.
corruption_summary: Irreverence is counted a small fault beside cruelty, and Romans puts ungodliness before unrighteousness in the indictment.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:18 sets the order of the charge, and the order is the doctrine: ungodliness first, then unrighteousness. The modern conscience reverses it, treating cruelty to men as the real sin and irreverence toward God as a private eccentricity that harms no one. Paul's argument through the rest of the chapter is that the second follows from the first — that a race which will not glorify God or be thankful is given over, by three separate acts of judicial abandonment, to the moral collapse the chapter then catalogues. Impiety is not the harmless half of the indictment. It is the root of the other half.

Psalm 36:1 gives the anatomy: the transgression of the wicked saith within my heart, that there is no fear of God before his eyes. The fear is not merely absent; it is absent before his eyes, which is to say the man has arranged his sight so that God is not in it. Romans 1:21 names the two withheld duties precisely — they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful — and both are omissions. Impiety rarely announces itself as blasphemy. It is usually a life in which God is simply not consulted, and the ingratitude of it is the part Scripture presses.

Hebrews 12:28 gives the answer, and it is not solemnity for its own sake: we receive a kingdom which cannot be moved, and therefore serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear — the reverence follows from the gift. Where reverence has to be manufactured it turns into the very superstition the Reformers fought; where the kingdom is actually received, it comes on its own, and the next clause tells why it is fitting: for our God is a consuming fire.
roots_summary: Greek asebeia (G763), ungodliness, impiety; asebes (G765), ungodly; eulabeia (G2124), godly fear, reverence; Hebrew pachad (H6343), dread, the fear of God.
roots_lines: Greek asebeia (G763) — ungodliness, impiety; Romans 1:18, 11:26, 2 Timothy 2:16, Titus 2:12, Jude 1:15, 1:18.
Greek eulabeia (G2124) — godly fear, reverence; Hebrews 5:7, 12:28.
Hebrew pachad Elohim (H6343, H430) — the fear of God; Psalm 36:1, Genesis 20:11.
usage: “Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” — the order of the indictment.
“They glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” — two omissions, and the collapse that followed.
“No fear of God before his eyes” — the sight arranged to exclude Him.

pos: adj. (contrary to law; not permitted; rendering Greek athemitos and anomos)
etymology: Un + lawful. The Greek of Acts 10:28 is athemitos, contrary to what is established — and the thing Peter calls unlawful there is a rule of men, not of God.
biblical_def: Peter in the house of Cornelius: “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Act 10:28). Of Lot in Sodom: that righteous man “vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds” (2Pe 2:8). The Lord answered the sabbath charge — “Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day” (Mat 12:2) — from David and the shewbread and from the priests in the temple, and concluded, “it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days” (Mat 12:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unlawful as not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law; and, of an act, contrary to the moral law or divine command.
webster_full: UNLAWFUL, a. Not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law; as an unlawful act.
2. Not moral; contrary to the divine law.
3. Illegitimate; born out of wedlock.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
(For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)
Mat 12:2
But when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day.
How much then is a man better than a sheep? Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days.
All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.
corruption_summary: Human rules are enforced as divine law, and Peter calls the rule that kept him out of Cornelius's house unlawful in exactly that sense.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 10:28 is a careful sentence and the care is easy to miss. Peter says it is an unlawful thing for a Jew to keep company with a Gentile — and no such law exists in Moses. It was a fence, a scruple built up around the clean and unclean legislation, held so long and so universally that it had the force of divine command in the conscience of every Jew in the room, Peter included, until the sheet came down three times. The passage is therefore the standing warning about the tradition that has hardened into law: sincerity is no protection, near-unanimity is no protection, and it took a vision repeated three times to move an apostle off it.

The Lord's sabbath controversies work the same seam. The Pharisees said not lawful of plucking corn and of healing, and He met them with Scripture rather than with sentiment — David ate the shewbread, the priests profane the sabbath and are blameless, and the sabbath was made for man. The lawful and the unlawful are decided by the Lawgiver and are found in the text; where the text is silent the conscience is free, and a church that binds it there has usurped a jurisdiction.

First Corinthians 6:12 guards the other flank, and Paul is quoting a slogan the Corinthians had got from him and stretched: all things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient. Liberty is real and it is not the last word; the free man asks not only whether a thing is permitted but whether it profits and whether it will bring him under its power. Between the fence that binds where God has not and the licence that will not ask a second question, the New Testament walks a narrow road.
roots_summary: Greek athemitos (G111), contrary to what is laid down, unlawful; anomos (G459), lawless, without law; exestin (G1832), it is lawful, permitted.
roots_lines: Greek athemitos (G111) — unlawful; Acts 10:28, 1 Peter 4:3 only.
Greek anomos (G459) — lawless, unlawful; 2 Peter 2:8, 1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.
Greek exestin (G1832) — it is lawful; Matthew 12:2, 12:10, 12:12, 1 Corinthians 6:12, 10:23.
usage: “It is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew” — a rule with no verse behind it.
“It is lawful to do well on the sabbath days” — the Lawgiver settling His own law.
“All things are lawful… but all things are not expedient” — the second question.

pos: adj. (pertaining to the church, its officers and government)
etymology: Greek ekklesia, an assembly called out, from ek, out, and kaleo, to call; through Latin ecclesiasticus. The church is named for a summons.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastical describes whatever belongs to the church as an institution — its officers, its assemblies, its discipline, its government. The root is the word the Lord chose: “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18), an ekklesia, a body called out. Its officers are elders and deacons (Php 1:1), appointed “in every city” (Tit 1:5); its assembly has authority to bind and loose (Mat 18:17–18); and its whole order exists “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” (Eph 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ecclesiastical as pertaining or relating to the church; not civil; as ecclesiastical polity, ecclesiastical courts, ecclesiastical history.
webster_full: ECCLESIASTICAL, a. Pertaining or relating to the church; not civil; as ecclesiastical jurisdiction or duties; ecclesiastical history; an ecclesiastical council.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Eph 4:12
For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:
Php 1:1
Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:
corruption_summary: Church order is treated as optional scaffolding, and the New Testament gives officers, assemblies and discipline before it gives a single building.
corruption_paragraphs: The word sounds institutional and the modern ear distrusts it, but the New Testament is unembarrassed about ecclesiastical matters: it names offices and their qualifications at length, orders that elders be ordained in every city, gives a procedure for discipline with three steps and an outcome, regulates the Supper, the collection, the widows' roll, and the conduct of the assembly down to the question of who speaks and in what order. A Christianity that keeps the doctrine and discards the polity has discarded a good deal of the New Testament's actual content.

The opposite corruption is to make the institution the thing itself. Ecclesiastical machinery can run for a long time with nothing inside it, and the church at Sardis had a name that it lived and was dead. The Reformed test is the marks: the Word truly preached, the ordinances rightly administered, and discipline exercised. Where those are, the church is, however plain its arrangements; where they are gone, no apostolic pedigree, no episcopal succession, and no constitution will supply them.

The root word settles the question of ownership. An ekklesia is a body summoned by someone, and the summons is Christ's; He said my church, and the officers of Ephesians 4 are His gifts to it. That is why ecclesiastical authority is real and strictly derivative: elders rule, and they rule by a Word they did not write, over a people they did not purchase, in a house that is not theirs.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly called out; presbuteros (G4245), elder; diakonos (G1249), deacon; oikodome (G3619), edifying, building up.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — church, assembly; Matthew 16:18, 18:17, Acts 20:28, Ephesians 5:25.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder; Titus 1:5, Acts 14:23, 1 Timothy 5:17; diakonos (G1249), Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:8.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — edifying; Ephesians 4:12, 4:16, 1 Corinthians 14:12.
usage: “Upon this rock I will build my church” — the possessive settles the ownership.
“Ordain elders in every city” — polity given, not left to taste.
“For the edifying of the body of Christ” — what the order is for.

pos: adj. (violating what is sacred; robbing holy things; rendering Greek hierosuleo, to commit sacrilege)
etymology: Latin sacrilegus, from sacer, sacred, and legere, to gather or steal — literally a temple-robber. The Greek hierosulos is the same picture.
biblical_def: To be sacrilegious is to lay hands on what belongs to God. Paul presses the charge on the man who boasts of the law: “Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?” (Rom 2:22). The town clerk at Ephesus certified that Paul's companions were “neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess” (Act 19:37). Achan took of the accursed thing and Israel could not stand before her enemies (Jos 7:11–12). Belshazzar drank from the temple vessels and the writing came out on the wall that night (Dan 5:3–5). Malachi puts it as a question: “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sacrilegious as violating sacred things; polluted with the crime of sacrilege; profane; impious.
webster_full: SACRILEGIOUS, a. Violating sacred things; polluted with the crime of sacrilege.
2. Containing sacrilege; partaking of the crime of sacrilege; profane; impious.
scriptures: Rom 2:22
Thou that sayest a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?
Mal 3:8
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
Dan 5:3
Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them.
Jos 7:11

Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff.
For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess.
corruption_summary: Sacrilege is imagined as vandalism in a cathedral, and Malachi charges it against men who kept back a tithe.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 3:8 asks the question in the plainest possible form — will a man rob God? — and answers it against a congregation that was still attending, still sacrificing, and still asking wherein have we robbed thee. The answer given is tithes and offerings: not a smashed altar, not a stolen vessel, but a withheld portion. Sacrilege in Scripture is far more often a quiet subtraction than a violent act, and the men charged with it are usually inside the building.

Romans 2:22 finds the same thing in a subtler place. Paul is addressing the Jew who abhors idols — genuinely, on principle — and asks whether he commits sacrilege, probably of trafficking in what had been devoted to idols, certainly of profiting from what he claimed to detest. The pattern is permanent: a religion strict in its condemnations and loose about what it takes. Belshazzar's feast is the same sin without the hypocrisy, and it was the last hour of his kingdom.

The doctrine under all of it is that God has property. He devoted Jericho, He owns the tithe, He claims the vessels, He calls a day His own and a body His temple — “if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” (1Co 3:17). The modern reader who finds the whole category strange has usually stopped believing that anything is set apart, which is the condition in which sacrilege becomes invisible rather than impossible.
roots_summary: Greek hierosuleo (G2416), to rob temples, commit sacrilege; hierosulos (G2417), a temple-robber; Hebrew cherem (H2764), the devoted or accursed thing; qaba (H6906), to rob.
roots_lines: Greek hierosuleo (G2416) — to commit sacrilege; Romans 2:22 only; hierosulos (G2417), Acts 19:37 only.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — the devoted thing, accursed; Joshua 6:18, 7:1, 7:11–13.
Hebrew qaba (H6906) — to rob, defraud; Malachi 3:8–9, Proverbs 22:23.
usage: “Will a man rob God?” — asked of men who were still attending.
“Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?” — strict in condemnation, loose in taking.
“The temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” — the property in question now.

pos: n. (ancientness; former ages; the authority claimed for age; rendering Hebrew qadmah)
etymology: Latin antiquitas, from antiquus, ancient. In the controversies of the Reformation the word names an argument: that a doctrine is proved by having been believed a long time.
biblical_def: Isaiah uses the word of Tyre: “Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn” (Isa 23:7) — and the age of the city did not save it. Scripture commends the old paths where they are God's: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). It equally condemns the antiquity of an error: the fathers who tempted God in the wilderness are a warning, not a precedent (Psa 95:8–9), and “your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?” (Zec 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antiquity as ancient times; former ages; great age; the people of ancient times; and remains of ancient times.
webster_full: ANTIQUITY, n. Ancient times; former ages; times long since past.
2. The ancients; the people of ancient times.
3. Ancientness; great age; the quality of being ancient.
4. Remains of ancient times.
scriptures: Isa 23:7
Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Zec 1:5
Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?
Psa 95:8
Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: Age is offered as proof of truth, and Jeremiah's old paths are commended for being God's, not for being old.
corruption_paragraphs: The appeal to antiquity was Rome's strongest instinctive argument and it remains the most persuasive one: this is what has always been believed, and you are new. The Reformers answered it in two ways. First by disputing the history — showing that the practices in question were not primitive but medieval, and that the fathers they were charged with abandoning could be quoted against Trent. Second, and more fundamentally, by denying that age settles the question at all. Tradition is a witness and not a judge; the Bereans searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things Paul preached were so, and Paul was an apostle.

Jeremiah 6:16 is the verse most often quoted for the other side, and it does commend the old paths — but the sentence names the test in its middle clause: ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein. The antiquity and the goodness are two separate questions, and Jeremiah expects the enquirer to ask both. Mark 7:8 shows what happens when only the first is asked: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, and the tradition there was old, respected, and universally kept.

The Protestant version of the error is nostalgia — a settled conviction that some earlier decade of one's own denomination was the golden age, and that recovery means returning to it. Zechariah 1:5 is the cure, and it is bracing: your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever? The fathers are dead and the word is not; the next verse says the word took hold of them. What survives an age is what was true in it, and the only way to find that out is to go back past every antiquity to the text.
roots_summary: Hebrew qadmah (H6927), antiquity, former state; olam (H5769), long duration, ancient time; Greek paradosis (G3862), tradition, that which is handed down.
roots_lines: Hebrew qadmah (H6927) — antiquity, former state; Isaiah 23:7, Ezekiel 16:55.
Hebrew netivot olam (H5410, H5769) — the old paths, ancient ways; Jeremiah 6:16, 18:15.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition; Mark 7:8–9, Colossians 2:8, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
usage: “Whose antiquity is of ancient days” — and her feet carried her away.
“Ask for the old paths, where is the good way” — two questions, not one.
“Your fathers, where are they?” — the cure for nostalgia.

pos: n. (rule exercised without right or without restraint; oppression by those in power)
etymology: Greek tyrannos, an absolute ruler who came to power outside the law; through Latin. The Reformers used the word constantly of a spiritual power binding consciences God has left free.
biblical_def: Tyranny is power exercised beyond right. Scripture describes it from both ends. Of the state: Samuel's warning of the king who “will take your sons… and your daughters… and ye shall cry out in that day because of your king” (1Sa 8:11–18), and Rehoboam's boast, “my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions” (1Ki 12:11). Of the church: “Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3), and “the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them… but it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:25–26). Of the conscience: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tyranny as arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; the exercise of power over subjects and others with a rigor not authorized by law or justice; cruel government; severity, rigorous command.
webster_full: TYRANNY, n. Arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; the exercise of power over subjects and others with a rigor not authorized by law or justice, or not requisite for the purposes of government.
2. Cruel government or discipline; as the tyranny of a master.
3. Severity; rigor; inclemency.
scriptures: And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots.
And now whereas my father did lade you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: Tyranny is looked for only in palaces, and the Reformers were more afraid of the kind that binds a conscience than the kind that taxes a purse.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation's characteristic use of the word was spiritual. Luther's treatise on the sacraments is called the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, and Calvin returns again and again to the tyranny of laws imposed on consciences Christ has freed — not because the burdens were physically heavy but because they were binding where God had not bound. The Confession draws the conclusion in a sentence: God alone is Lord of the conscience, and has left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in any thing contrary to His Word, or beside it in matters of faith or worship. The phrase or beside it is the whole Reformation.

Civil tyranny is treated soberly and without romance. Samuel's speech in 1 Samuel 8 is a list of what a king will take, delivered by God's own prophet to a people determined to have one anyway, and it ends with the sentence that ye shall cry out in that day and the LORD will not hear you in that day. The state's overreach is real and is often a judgment. But Romans 13 stands beside it, and the Reformed tradition has generally refused both the divine right of kings and the right of private revolt, locating resistance where it belongs, in the lesser magistrate and in the plain refusal to obey a command that contradicts God.

The subtlest tyranny is the one inside the church, and Peter names it in the middle of an exhortation to elders: feed the flock, taking the oversight, neither as being lords over God's heritage. The heritage is God's, which is what makes the lordship theft; and the word is set against being ensamples to the flock, which is what an elder is instead. A ministry that governs by pressure, by access, or by the manufactured conscience of a congregation afraid to disagree has become what Peter forbade, however sound its doctrinal statement.
roots_summary: Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to lord it over, exercise dominion against; katexousiazo (G2715), to exercise authority upon; Hebrew ashaq (H6231), to oppress; perek (H6531), rigour.
roots_lines: Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; Matthew 20:25, Mark 10:42, 1 Peter 5:3, Acts 19:16.
Greek katexousiazo (G2715) — to exercise authority over; Matthew 20:25, Mark 10:42.
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud; Ecclesiastes 4:1, Micah 2:2; perek (H6531), rigour; Exodus 1:13–14, Leviticus 25:43.
usage: “Ye shall cry out in that day because of your king” — Samuel's warning, delivered and ignored.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” — the heritage is God's, which makes it theft.
“Be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” — the tyranny the Reformers feared most.

pos: n. (want of thankfulness; the failure to return acknowledgment for benefits received)
etymology: Latin ingratitudo, from in, not, and gratus, thankful, pleasing — the same root as grace. Ingratitude is, etymologically, gracelessness.
biblical_def: Ingratitude is the refusal of thanks. Paul makes it one of the two hinges on which the case against mankind turns: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom 1:21). It is a mark of the last days: men shall be “unthankful, unholy” (2Ti 3:2). Moses charges it as the folly of a redeemed people: “Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee?” (Deu 32:6). Nine lepers healed did not return; one did, and the Lord asked, “Where are the nine?” (Luk 17:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ingratitude as want of gratitude; insensibility to favors, and want of a disposition to repay them; unthankfulness.
webster_full: INGRATITUDE, n. Want of gratitude; insensibility to favors, and want of a disposition to repay them; unthankfulness.
scriptures: Rom 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Deu 32:6
Do ye thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?
And Jesus answering said, Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?
They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt;
corruption_summary: Ingratitude is filed among small faults, and Romans makes it one of the two hinges on which the darkening of the world turned.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:21 is the most consequential sentence about ingratitude ever written, and its structure repays attention. They knew God — the knowledge is granted — and then two failures: they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful. From those two omissions everything else in the chapter follows: vain imaginations, a darkened heart, professed wisdom, and the exchange of the glory of the uncorruptible God for an image. Ingratitude is not listed among the consequences of the fall; it stands at the head of the descent, and the idolatry and the moral collapse come after it.

Luke 17 supplies the numbers. Ten lepers cried for mercy, ten were told to go and shew themselves to the priests, and ten were cleansed as they went; one turned back, glorified God with a loud voice, and fell down on his face giving thanks — and he was a Samaritan. The Lord's question is not rhetorical filler: were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? Nine men had received the greatest mercy of their lives and simply went on with the afternoon, and nothing suggests they were wicked men. That is the ordinary shape of ingratitude: not a refusal, an omission.

Deuteronomy 32:6 gives the reason it is worse than an omission. Do ye thus requite the LORD — and then three grounds, each of them a claim: is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee? Creation, redemption, preservation. Where those three are true of a man, thanklessness is not merely bad manners; it is a lie told with the whole life about who he is and where he came from, and Psalm 106:21 says of Israel exactly what it says of every unthankful heart: they forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt.
roots_summary: Greek eucharisteo (G2168), to give thanks; acharistos (G884), unthankful; Hebrew gamal (H1580), to requite, deal out; shakach (H7911), to forget.
roots_lines: Greek eucharisteo (G2168) — to give thanks; Romans 1:21, Luke 17:16, 1 Thessalonians 5:18.
Greek acharistos (G884) — unthankful; Luke 6:35, 2 Timothy 3:2 only.
Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to requite; Deuteronomy 32:6, Psalm 116:12; shakach (H7911), to forget; Psalm 106:21.
usage: “Neither were thankful” — one of the two omissions the descent began with.
“Where are the nine?” — ordinary ingratitude, and not one of them wicked.
“Is not he thy father that hath bought thee?” — three grounds in one verse.
